title: A Controlled Null Result for Per-Gate Riemannian Optimization in VQE
abstract: Parametrized gates in a variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) live on a product of unitary groups, which makes Riemannian optimization a natural candidate for improving training. We test this candidate in the clean per-gate setting: each single-qubit gate is optimized directly on U (2) and compared with Adam on an unconstrained Euler-angle chart representing the same physical gate, initialized from the same unitaries and tuned with a separate learning-rate sweep. On a validated hydrogen-chain benchmark, we find no measurable practical advantage from the Riemannian machinery. The direct manifold optimizer and the Euler-coordinate baseline are interleaved in final error and success rate; the classical coordinate baseline is not slower in iterations on the successful cells; and the choices of Riemannian metric, retraction, and momentum vector transport do not change the conclusion. We also identify four failure modes that can manufacture an apparent positive result: a trivial product-state benchmark, a projected-matrix Adam baseline that discards most of its own step, a non-unitary inherited Cayley retraction that lets the reported energy pass below the variational minimum, and a learning-rate grid whose optimum sits at its boundary. Each failure mode produced a plausible multi-seed result in our own workflow before being caught. The practical output of this paper is therefore a controlled null result and a validation checklist for VQE optimizer comparisons.
summary: This paper investigates whether using Riemannian geometry to optimize individual gates in VQE circuits improves performance over standard optimization methods. Through rigorous testing on a hydrogen-chain benchmark, the authors report a controlled null result, finding no practical advantage. The main contribution is establishing a detailed validation checklist to guide future, more reliable comparisons of quantum optimizers.
main_problem: To rigorously test whether optimizing variational quantum circuits using per-gate Riemannian optimization offers a practical advantage over standard classical optimizers like Adam.
main_result: The study concludes a controlled null result, finding no measurable practical advantage for Riemannian optimization over a matched Euler-angle Adam baseline on a validated hydrogen-chain benchmark.
method: The authors compare Riemannian optimization techniques (using various retractions and metrics) against a classical Adam baseline applied to the same physical gates, using a rigorous validation protocol.
model_or_system: The model is the Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) applied to neutral hydrogen chains. The ansatz involves trainable single-qubit U(2) gates followed by a fixed CNOT entangler.
key_observables: Geometric mean best energy error (|E - \lambda_min|) and success rate at chemical accuracy (1.6 x 10^-3 Ha). Diagnostics include Schmidt rank and half-chain entropy.
important_parameters: The comparison is restricted to the clean per-gate U(2) setting, excluding noisy hardware or large-block compilation.
main_assumptions: The primary limitation is the scope: the result is only valid for the specific per-gate U(2) regime tested, and the paper provides a checklist for future comparisons.
figures_summary: Figures compare the performance of Euler-coordinate Adam versus direct per-gate manifold Adam, while tables summarize performance metrics and list four identified failure modes that can create false positives.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem, details the Riemannian optimization methods and baselines, presents results on the hydrogen-chain benchmark showing no advantage, and concludes by detailing four failure modes and proposing a validation checklist for future work.
why_interesting: It provides a crucial, highly technical benchmark and validation checklist for the entire field of quantum machine learning optimization, helping researchers avoid misleading positive results.

figures.caption: FIGURE 1. Depth calibration used before ranking optimizers. Operating points are chosen near the shallowest depths that can reach chemical accuracy; cells that no tested method can solve are not used as evidence for optimizer superiority.

FIGURE 2. Matched Euler-coordinate Adam versus direct per-gate manifold Adam. Dots denote individual seeds and lines denote the geometric mean at the best learning rate per method. The two valid methods are interleaved; projected matrix Adam sits far above both.

FIGURE 3. Ingredient and failure-mode ablations. The safe geometric choices do not separate in the resolved cells; apparent large effects arise from invalid baselines, unsafe retractions, or insufficient learning-rate grids.
